stops.name: Public Square
stops.description: The ten-acre plaza Cleveland was laid out around in 1796, and the point every other stop on this walk is measured from.

stops.name: Cuyahoga County Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument
stops.description: Dedicated on the Fourth of July 1894 to the more than 9,000 Cuyahoga County men who served the Union, and designed by Levi Scofield, a Civil War veteran himself.

stops.name: Terminal Tower
stops.description: Finished in 1927 on top of a working railroad terminal, this 52-story tower was the second-tallest building in the world at the time and the tallest in North America outside New York City until 1964.

stops.name: Hotel Cleveland
stops.description: Open since 1918 and now folded into the Tower City complex beside it, this is the last of the grand Public Square hotels still taking guests.

stops.name: Old Stone Church
stops.description: Built in 1855, this Presbyterian sanctuary is the oldest building standing on Public Square and has outlasted every skyscraper that grew up around it.

stops.name: The Arcade
stops.description: A 300-foot glass-roofed shopping arcade opened in 1890, among the earliest indoor malls in the country and a National Historic Landmark since 1975.

stops.name: Cleveland Trust Company Building
stops.description: George B. Post's 1907 bank, whose stained-glass rotunda now shelters a downtown grocery store instead of tellers.

stops.name: Playhouse Square
stops.description: Five theaters built in the early 1920s, all of them dark by the end of the 1960s, saved by a grassroots campaign that left Cleveland with the largest performing arts center outside New York.

stops.name: Cleveland Public Library Main Library
stops.description: The main library on the Mall, built as part of the Group Plan civic center and still the front door of a 27-branch system founded in 1869.

stops.name: Fountain of Eternal Life
stops.description: Marshall Fredericks' bronze figure rising out of the flames of war, dedicated on Memorial Day 1964 as the city's memorial to its war dead.

stops.name: Cuyahoga County Courthouse
stops.description: A Beaux Arts courthouse finished in 1912 under the 1903 Group Plan, its interior carrying murals by Frank Brangwyn and Violet Oakley.

stops.name: Cleveland City Hall
stops.description: J. Milton Dyer's 1916 seat of city government, whose rotunda holds a copy of Archibald Willard's painting The Spirit of '76.

stops.name: Free Stamp
stops.description: Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen's 49-foot rubber stamp, commissioned by Standard Oil, rejected by its successor BP, and finally set on its side in Willard Park in 1991 so the word FREE reads to the street.

stops.name: Public Auditorium
stops.description: A 1922 civic hall seating 10,000 that has hosted two Republican National Conventions and now serves as home court for the Cleveland Charge.

stops.name: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
stops.description: I. M. Pei's glass pyramid on the Lake Erie shore, dedicated in 1995 after Cleveland won a long campaign to host it.

note: Cleveland had never been run. The sweep was a 2 km Wikipedia GeoSearch off Public Square (199 geotagged pages) narrowed against the NRHP Cuyahoga County listings and the Cleveland Mall historic district; every stop was opened individually and confirmed still standing. The loop is tight: Public Square, east along Euclid to Playhouse Square, back up E 9th to the Mall and Lakeside, then north to the lakefront, roughly 1.2 miles end to end with the Rock Hall as the far anchor. All 15 stops carry a verified ZIP. Three have no street address and are null rather than guessed: Public Square itself (the plaza, not a numbered lot), the Fountain of Eternal Life (Memorial Plaza on the Mall, off West Mall Dr), and the Free Stamp (Willard Park at E 9th and Lakeside, whose only civic address is City Hall's next door). ZIPs were checked against the Census geocoder and cross-checked in Nominatim; note that the Census geocoder returns a bogus 44141 for Public Square house numbers, so 44113 there comes from the cross-check and the Old Stone Church infobox. Two verified stops were cut to hold the 15 cap, both a little south of the loop and both worth adding if you want more: Grays Armory, 1234 Bolivar Rd, 44115 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grays_Armory), an 1894 private militia armory still run as a museum, and Erie Street Cemetery, 2254 E 9th St, 44115 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erie_Street_Cemetery), an 1826 burying ground with 17,000 interments including Revolutionary War veterans. Dropped from the sweep: Cleveland Stadium and the Hollenden Hotel (demolished), Sokolowski's University Inn (closed), and West Side Market (real and excellent, but 1.5 miles across the river in Ohio City and an outlier on a downtown walk).
